Pattern 09 of 24

Modified Binary Search

Each question you ask throws away half of the remaining possibilities. Once you see that "yes/no" boundary, a million candidates take only 20 checks.

A 6-minute conversation: Sam asks, Priya explains
0:00 / 6:28
  1. Sam Binary search. I know the basic idea, but the page is called modified binary search. What's modified about it?
  2. Priya The basic version finds a number in a sorted list. The modified version plays the same game on things that don't look like a sorted list at all: a rotated array, a mountain, or even the answer itself. The page's summary is that each question you ask throws away half of what's left, so a million candidates take about twenty checks.
  3. Sam Twenty checks for a million. That's the power of halving.
  4. Priya And the real skill isn't the halving. It's spotting where the halving applies.
  5. Priya Think of the "guess my number between one and a hundred" game. Nobody sensible guesses one, two, three. You guess fifty. "Higher." Seventy-five. "Lower." Each answer cuts what's left in half, so you win in seven guesses or fewer.
  6. Sam So binary search is that game.
  7. Priya Yes. And what interviews really test is whether you can see a yes-or-no boundary: a row of noes followed by a row of yeses. If that boundary exists, binary search finds it. It might be "is this number at least the target?", or "is this speed fast enough?" The array doesn't even have to exist. You can search over a range of possible answers.
  8. Sam How do I set one up?
  9. Priya First, define the search space: either the positions in an array, or the range of possible answers, from the smallest to the largest. Second, define the yes-or-no question, and check it only flips once. Once it says yes, it keeps saying yes.
  10. Sam Then look at the middle.
  11. Priya Right. If the middle says yes, the first yes is at the middle or to its left, so the high end moves to the middle. If it says no, the first yes is strictly to the right, so the low end moves to one past the middle. Stop when low and high meet. That's your answer.
  12. Sam And the "modified" part is just a smarter question?
  13. Priya Exactly. For a rotated array, the question is "which half is sorted, and is the target inside it?" For "minimise the maximum," the question is a quick simulation: "can I do it with a limit of x?"
  14. Sam The page has an example about bananas.
  15. Priya Koko eats bananas. There are piles of three, six, seven and eleven, and she has eight hours. What's the slowest eating speed that finishes in time? You don't search the piles. You search the possible speeds, one to eleven. "Is this speed fast enough?" is no, no, no, then yes, yes, yes. Find the first yes.
  16. Sam How do I spot these?
  17. Priya "Sorted array," "rotated sorted array," "first or last position." The phrase "in O(log n) time" is a huge hint. "Minimum speed, capacity or days such that something works." "Minimise the maximum." "Peak element," "square root," "first bad version."
  18. Sam And the one question?
  19. Priya If I guess an answer x, can I quickly tell whether the real answer is bigger or smaller? If yes, it's binary search, even when there's no array in sight.
  20. Priya Your turn. "Ship all packages within D days. What's the minimum ship capacity?" Which pattern?
  21. Priya Binary search on the answer. A bigger ship always works if a smaller one does, so it's no, no, then yes. Search capacities from the heaviest single package up to the total weight, and check each guess by simulating the days.
  22. Sam When is it the wrong tool?
  23. Priya If the data is unsorted and you only need to look once, just scan it. Sorting first costs more than scanning. If the feasibility check isn't monotonic, binary search silently returns garbage, and you probably need dynamic programming. And for pair sums on a sorted array, two pointers is simpler.
  24. Sam Template A, lower bound.
  25. Priya It finds the first position whose value is at least the target, which is also where the target would be inserted. The section's hook is guessing a page in a dictionary. If the word on the page comes before yours, that page and everything before it are out. Otherwise, this page might be the first one with your word, so you keep it.
  26. Sam The page makes a big deal of "half-open" ranges.
  27. Priya Because the details travel together. Low starts at zero, high starts at the length of the array, one past the end. Loop while low is less than high. Too small, low becomes mid plus one. Otherwise, high becomes mid. If you mix that with the other style, you get off-by-one errors or infinite loops.
  28. Sam Template B?
  29. Priya First true, or binary search on the answer. It's template A with the array replaced by any yes-or-no test. Koko's bananas, ship capacity, split array.
  30. Sam And C is the rotated array.
  31. Priya At any cut of a rotated sorted array, at least one half is still in order. So you check which half is sorted, then ask whether the target lies inside that half's range. If yes, search there. If not, search the other half.
  32. Priya Quick check. The loop is "while low is less than high," and if the middle passes, high becomes mid. What goes in the other branch?
  33. Priya Low becomes mid plus one. The middle failed, so it can't be the answer. If you wrote low equals mid, then when low and high are next to each other, mid equals low forever, and you loop forever.
  34. Sam The memory hook?
  35. Priya "Find the first yes." Every binary search problem is a row of noes followed by a row of yeses. Your only job is to write the question and find the first yes. The picture is a row of light switches, all off, then all on. You're blindfolded, you test the middle switch, and you throw away the half that can't hold the first one that's on.
  36. Sam And the chant?
  37. Priya Low less than high. Mid in the middle. Yes, high is mid. No, low is mid plus one.
  38. Sam Mistakes?
  39. Priya The infinite loop we just covered. Mixing the half-open and closed styles. A search range that doesn't surely contain the answer: for split array, starting at zero makes the check meaningless, it has to start at the biggest single number. A check that isn't monotonic. And using floating-point ceiling division, when an integer trick avoids rounding errors.
  40. Sam Where do I start?
  41. Priya Binary search, then search insert position, then first bad version. They're marked "start here." Then Koko eating bananas, which is the gateway to binary search on the answer.
  42. Sam Next on the path?
  43. Priya Fast and slow pointers, back on linked lists. Two runners at different speeds, and a surprisingly beautiful proof.

1. What is this pattern for?

Think of the "guess my number between 1 and 100" game. Nobody smart guesses 1, 2, 3… You guess 50. "Higher." Now 75. "Lower." Each answer cuts what's left in half, so you always win in 7 guesses or fewer. Binary search is that game, and "modified" binary search means playing it on things that don't look like a sorted list at first: a rotated array, a mountain, or even the answer itself ("what's the slowest speed that still finishes on time?").

Classic binary search finds a value in a sorted array in O(log n). The real skill, and what interviews test, is noticing a monotonic yes/no boundary:

index / candidate:  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
condition true?  :  F  F  F  F  T  T  T  T     ← find the FIRST T

If such a boundary exists, binary search finds it. It might be "nums[i] ≥ target" (lower bound), "this element is in the rotated part", or "speed k is fast enough" (binary search on the answer). The array doesn't even have to exist: you can binary search over a range of possible answers.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Define the search space. Either indices [0, n) of an array, or a range of candidate answers [lo, hi] (smallest to largest possible answer).
  2. Define the yes/no question ok(x), and make sure it's monotonic: once it turns True, it stays True (F F F T T T).
  3. Look at the middle: mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
  4. Keep the half that can still contain the answer. If ok(mid), the first True is at mid or to its left, so hi = mid. Otherwise it's strictly to the right, so lo = mid + 1.
  5. Stop when the window is empty (lo == hi). lo is the first True. Each step halves the window, so it's O(log n) steps.
  6. "Modified" = a smarter question. For a rotated array, first decide which half is sorted, then check whether the target lies inside it. For "minimize the maximum", ok(x) is a greedy simulation: "can I do it with limit x?"

Binary search on the answer. Koko eats bananas at speed k piles-per-hour (one pile per hour at most). Piles [3, 6, 7, 11], 8 hours. The array we search is the list of possible speeds 1..11. "Is speed k fast enough?" is F F F T T T…, so we find the first T.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot Modified Binary Search

Trigger words

  • "sorted array", "rotated sorted array", "find first / last position"
  • "in O(log n)" (a huge hint)
  • "minimum speed / capacity / days such that…", "minimize the maximum", "maximize the minimum"
  • "k-th smallest" in a sorted matrix / multiplication table / pairs
  • "peak element", "mountain array", "square root", "first bad version"

Shape of the input

  • Sorted (or piecewise-sorted) data, or a numeric answer inside a known range [lo, hi].
  • You can write a check(x) whose results flip only once (F→T).
  • Constraints like n ≤ 10⁵ and values up to 10⁹: values too big to try one by one, but log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30 tries is nothing.
  • The brute force tries every index or every candidate answer: O(n) or O(range × n).
The one question to ask"If I guess an answer x, can I quickly tell whether the real answer is bigger or smaller than x?" If yes, binary search, even when there's no array in sight.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use Binary Search when…Prefer something else when…
The data is sorted (even if rotated) and you need a position or a valueThe data is unsorted and you only need it once: a linear scan (O(n)) beats sorting (O(n log n))
"Minimum X such that it's feasible", where feasibility is monotonicFeasibility isn't monotonic, or choices interact: use Dynamic Programming
Pair-sum / triplet problems on a sorted array, one element at a timeUsually Two Pointers is simpler and O(n) instead of O(n log n)
k-th smallest when you can count "how many ≤ x" fastk-th largest of an unsorted stream: use a heap (Top K Elements)
Subarray with a property and all-positive numbers, searched by lengthA Sliding Window usually does it in O(n)

Cost: O(log n) comparisons on an array, O(1) space. Binary search on the answer: O(log(range) × cost of check), e.g. O(n log(max)) for Koko and Split Array.

5. The templates, step by step (Python, TypeScript, Java)

Binary search has three templates. All halve a range each step; they differ in what the range means. A (lower bound) finds the first index whose value is ≥ target in a sorted array, using a half-open range [low, high). B (first true) is A with the array replaced by any yes/no test that flips from no to yes once: "binary search on the answer". C searches a rotated sorted array, using the fact that at least one half is always sorted.

Template A · Lower bound: first index with nums[i] ≥ target

The question it answersWhere is the first value ≥ target (also: where would target be inserted)?
What it keepsA half-open range [low, high) that always contains the answer.
When it checks for an answerEnds when low == high: that's the answer.
Use it whenFirst/last position of a value, insert position, count of values < x, floor/ceiling.
Not forUnsorted data; "any index that matches" is fine with this too, but it doesn't stop early.
Memory hook: "Too small → the answer is to the right of mid; otherwise mid might be it"Guessing a page in a dictionary: if the word on the page comes before yours, every page up to it is out (low = mid + 1). Otherwise this page could be the first one with your word, so keep it (high = mid).

The story, mapped to the code. The array is a sorted dictionary; the answer is the first page that isn't before your word.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Pages still possible[low, high)Half-open: high itself is a valid answer ("after the end").
Open the middle pagemid = (low + high) // 2Always < high, so it's a real index.
Page is before my wordnums[mid] < target → low = mid + 1mid and everything left of it are out.
Page might be the firstelse high = midKeep mid as a candidate.
One page leftlow == highThe answer.

The template. Note high = len(nums) and while low < high: the two choices go together.

def lower_bound(nums, target):
    low, high = 0, len(nums)
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if nums[mid] < target:
            low = mid + 1
        else:
            high = mid
    return low
function lowerBound(nums: number[], target: number): number {
  let low = 0, high = nums.length;
  while (low < high) {
    const mid = (low + high) >> 1;
    if (nums[mid] < target) {
      low = mid + 1;
    } else {
      high = mid;
    }
  }
  return low;
}
static int lowerBound(int[] nums, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = nums.length;
    while (low < high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] < target) {
            low = mid + 1;
        } else {
            high = mid;
        }
    }
    return low;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
low, high = 0, len(nums)The answer can be any index 0..n (n = "after everything").All pages, plus "after the last page".high = len - 1 can never answer "insert at the end".
while low < highStop when one candidate is left.One page left.<= with high = mid loops forever when low == high.
mid = (low + high) // 2Rounds down, so mid < high.Open the middle page.In Java/C++ write low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid overflow.
low = mid + 1mid is too small; drop it.This page and earlier are out.low = mid can loop forever when high = low + 1.
high = midmid could be the answer; keep it.Keep this page.high = mid - 1 throws away a valid answer (see the bug player).

Watch it run. Step through nums = [1, 3, 5, 5, 8], target = 5. The second player mixes in high = mid - 1.

high = mid - 1 belongs to the closed-range style. Mixed into this template, it throws away index 2 (the answer) and returns 1.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. Everything before low is < target; everything at or after high is ≥ target. When they meet, low is the first index ≥ target.

Complexity. O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Mixing closed and half-open styles. Half-open: high = len, low < high, high = mid.
  • low = mid. mid was checked and is too small: mid + 1.
  • Assuming the target exists. Check low < len and nums[low] == target.
Recall card
Memory hook
Too small → right of mid; otherwise mid might be it.
Choose this template when
First position / insert position / count less than → lower bound.
Invariant
Left of low: < target. From high on: ≥ target.
The line people get wrong
high = mid (not mid − 1).

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

lower_bound([1,3,5,5,8], 9)?

5 (after the end).

Last position of 5?

lower_bound(nums, 6) − 1 = 3.

Count of values < 5?

lower_bound(nums, 5) = 2.

Template B · First true (binary search on the answer)

The question it answersWhat's the smallest x in [low, high] for which is_ok(x) is true, if is_ok flips from false to true once?
What it keepsA half-open range of candidate answers.
When it checks for an answerEach step asks is_ok(mid) once.
Use it whenMinimum capacity/speed/time that works (Koko, ship packages), smallest x with x² ≥ n, first bad version.
Not forTests that flip more than once (not monotonic).
Memory hook: "Find the first yes on a no-no-no-yes-yes line"Lay out every possible answer on a line. The test says no, no, no… then yes forever. Binary search finds the first yes: a yes means the answer is here or to the left; a no means it's to the right.

The story, mapped to the code. Each candidate answer is a door; behind the first door that opens is the answer.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Candidate answerslow..highAll possible values of x.
Try a dooris_ok(mid)One test per step.
Openshigh = midAnswer is mid or smaller.
Stays shutlow = mid + 1Answer is bigger.
First door that opensreturn lowSmallest x with is_ok(x).

The template. Exactly A, with nums[mid] < target replaced by not is_ok(mid).

def first_true(low, high, is_ok):
    high += 1
    while low < high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if is_ok(mid):
            high = mid
        else:
            low = mid + 1
    return low
function firstTrue(low: number, high: number, isOk: (x: number) => boolean): number {
  high += 1;
  while (low < high) {
    const mid = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);
    if (isOk(mid)) {
      high = mid;
    } else {
      low = mid + 1;
    }
  }
  return low;
}
static int firstTrue(int low, int high, IntPredicate isOk) {
    high += 1;
    while (low < high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (isOk.test(mid)) {
            high = mid;
        } else {
            low = mid + 1;
        }
    }
    return low;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
high += 1Makes the range half-open; returning high + 1 means "no x works".An extra door meaning "none opened".Without it, a range where nothing works returns high as if it worked.
if is_ok(mid): high = midmid works; maybe something smaller does too.The door opens; look left.—
else: low = mid + 1mid fails, so everything ≤ mid fails.Shut; look right.This relies on monotonicity: no → all smaller are no.

Watch it run. Step through the smallest x in 1..10 with x * x >= 30.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. Every candidate before low fails; every candidate from high on passes (with high = original high + 1 as "none").

Complexity. O(log(range) × cost of is_ok).

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Non-monotonic test. It must be no…no, yes…yes.
  • Wrong range. low = smallest possible answer, high = largest possible (e.g., max(piles) for Koko).
  • Forgetting the "none" case. If the result is high + 1, nothing worked.
Recall card
Memory hook
Find the first yes on a no-no-yes-yes line.
Choose this template when
"Minimum X such that it works" with a monotonic check → B.
Invariant
Left of low: no. From high on: yes.
The line people get wrong
high = mid on yes.

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

Smallest x with x² ≥ 30 in 1..10?

6.

Koko: what's is_ok(speed)?

Hours needed at that speed ≤ h.

What does a result of high + 1 mean?

No candidate passed.

Template C · Search in a rotated sorted array

The question it answersFind target's index in a sorted array that was rotated (no duplicates), in O(log n).
What it keepsA closed range [low, high].
When it checks for an answerEach step: is mid the target? Which half is sorted? Is target inside it?
Use it whenLC 33 (and with care, LC 81 with duplicates); min of a rotated array is a cousin.
Not forPlain sorted arrays (A is simpler).
Memory hook: "One half is always sorted: check if the target lives there"A clock face rotated: cut it at the middle and at least one half reads in order. If target is inside that ordered half's range, search there; otherwise search the other half.

The story, mapped to the code. The array is a sorted bookshelf that someone rotated.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
The ordered halfnums[low] <= nums[mid] → left half sortedOtherwise the right half is.
Target inside the ordered halfnums[low] <= target < nums[mid]Range check on a sorted half is safe.
Go therehigh = mid - 1Or low = mid + 1 for the right half.
Foundnums[mid] == targetReturn mid.

The template. Closed range (high = len - 1, low <= high) because we return as soon as we see the target.

def search_rotated(nums, target):
    low, high = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[low] <= nums[mid]:
            if nums[low] <= target < nums[mid]:
                high = mid - 1
            else:
                low = mid + 1
        else:
            if nums[mid] < target <= nums[high]:
                low = mid + 1
            else:
                high = mid - 1
    return -1
function searchRotated(nums: number[], target: number): number {
  let low = 0, high = nums.length - 1;
  while (low <= high) {
    const mid = (low + high) >> 1;
    if (nums[mid] === target) {
      return mid;
    }
    if (nums[low] <= nums[mid]) {
      if (nums[low] <= target && target < nums[mid]) {
        high = mid - 1;
      } else {
        low = mid + 1;
      }
    } else {
      if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[high]) {
        low = mid + 1;
      } else {
        high = mid - 1;
      }
    }
  }
  return -1;
}
static int searchRotated(int[] nums, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = nums.length - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            return mid;
        }
        if (nums[low] <= nums[mid]) {
            if (nums[low] <= target && target < nums[mid]) {
                high = mid - 1;
            } else {
                low = mid + 1;
            }
        } else {
            if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[high]) {
                low = mid + 1;
            } else {
                high = mid - 1;
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
if nums[low] <= nums[mid]Is the left half sorted?Does the left half read in order?< fails when low == mid (two elements left), e.g. [3, 1] searching 1.
if nums[low] <= target < nums[mid]Is target inside the sorted left half?Is the book on the ordered shelf?Checking only target < nums[mid] ignores the rotation.
if nums[mid] < target <= nums[high]Same check for the sorted right half.——
return -1Range empty: not present.——

Watch it run. Step through nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. If target is in the array, its index is in [low, high]. Each step drops a half that provably doesn't contain it.

Complexity. O(log n) time, O(1) space (without duplicates; duplicates can force O(n)).

Mistakes this template invites:

  • nums[low] < nums[mid]. Use <=: low == mid makes a one-element sorted half.
  • Range-checking the unsorted half. Only the sorted half's range check is reliable.
Recall card
Memory hook
One half is always sorted: check if target lives there.
Choose this template when
Rotated sorted array → C.
Invariant
Target (if present) stays within [low, high].
The line people get wrong
nums[low] <= nums[mid] with <=.

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

Which half is sorted for low=0, mid=3 in [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]?

The left half [4,5,6,7].

Why closed range here?

We return as soon as nums[mid] == target.

Duplicates?

When nums[low] == nums[mid] == nums[high], shrink both ends by one.

Choosing between the templates

QuestionA · lower boundB · first trueC · rotated
Range styleHalf-open [low, high)Half-open (high + 1)Closed [low, high]
Looplow < highlow < highlow <= high
Moveslow = mid + 1 / high = midlow = mid + 1 / high = midlow = mid + 1 / high = mid − 1
ReturnsFirst index ≥ targetFirst x with is_ok(x)Index of target or −1
Typical promptLC 35, LC 34LC 875, 1011, 69, 278LC 33, 153

Default to the half-open style (A/B): it never loses an answer and returns a position even when the target is missing. Use the closed style (C) when you stop as soon as you hit the target. Never mix the two in one function.

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Find the first yes"Every binary search problem is a row of NOs followed by a row of YESes. Your only job is to write the yes/no question and find where the first YES is.
How this hook works: what “Find the first yes” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Find”
Binary search: test the middle and throw away the half that can't hold the answer.
“the first yes”
Write a yes/no question about each position. In every binary search problem the answers look like NO NO NO YES YES YES, and the answer you want is where the first YES is.

Why this picture fits the pattern: Binary search comes in many forms (lower bound, rotated arrays, peaks, "minimum speed that works"), and their off-by-ones are notorious. The hook reduces every version to one loop. The only creative part is choosing the question.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
The row of NOs then YESesthe range [low, high)
The yes/no questionnums[middle] >= target (or ok(middle))
YES: the first yes is here or to the lefthigh = middle
NO: the first yes is to the rightlow = middle + 1
Only one place leftloop ends at low == high

Watch it on numbers

Lower bound of 7 in nums = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]. Question: "is nums[i] >= 7?" The answers are N N N Y Y Y.

  1. low = 0, high = 6, middle = 3: 7 ≥ 7? YES, so high = 3.
  2. middle = 1: 3 ≥ 7? NO, so low = 2.
  3. middle = 2: 5 ≥ 7? NO, so low = 3.
  4. low == high == 3: the first yes is index 3.

The trap it saves you from

Mixing loop styles (low <= high with high = middle, or low = middle) leads to infinite loops and off-by-ones. With "find the first yes" there is one rule set: while low < high, YES → high = middle, NO → low = middle + 1.

It still works when…

Koko Eating Bananas: the question is "can she finish at speed s?" and the speeds run NO…YES. Rotated sorted array: "is nums[i] <= nums[-1]?" On [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] that's N N N N Y Y Y, and the first yes (index 4) is the minimum. Find Peak: "is nums[i] > nums[i + 1]?"

Picture

A row of light switches: all OFF, then all ON. You're blindfolded and can flip-test one switch at a time. Test the middle one, then throw away the half that can't hold the first ON switch.

Chant

"lo less than hi; mid in the middle; yes → hi is mid; no → lo is mid plus one."

On-the-answer cue

"Minimum something that still works?" → guess it, check it greedily, halve the range.

Each template, in the hook's words

Template (section 5)In the hook's wordsThe line that does it
A · Lower boundThe question is “is this number at least the target?” Find the first yes.if nums[mid] < target: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid
B · On the answerThe question is “does this answer work?” The answers are a row of nos, then yeses; find the first yes.if is_ok(mid): high = mid else: low = mid + 1
C · Rotated arrayOne half is always sorted; ask “is the target inside the sorted half?” and keep the half that says yes.if nums[low] <= nums[mid]: ...

Medium 33. Search in Rotated Sorted Array Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft Apple Array

Problem: A sorted array of distinct numbers was rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] → [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Find the index of target in O(log n), or return -1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target = 0
Output: 4
Example 2
Input: nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2], target = 3
Output: -1

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 5000 · -10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴ · All values of nums are unique. · nums is an ascending array that is possibly rotated. · -10⁴ ≤ target ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

Cut the array at mid. At least one of the two halves is still fully sorted.

Hint 2

Check whether the target lies inside the sorted half (a simple range test); if yes search there, otherwise search the other half.

From brute force to the pattern: A linear scan is O(n), but the problem asks for O(log n). Even after rotation, one half around mid is always sorted, so each step can still discard half the array: O(log n).

Spot it: "sorted" + "rotated" + "O(log n)" → modified binary search.

Key insight: Cut a rotated array anywhere and at least one half is perfectly sorted. Check which one (nums[lo] ≤ nums[mid] means the left half is sorted). In a sorted half you can tell instantly whether the target is inside by comparing with its two ends. If it is, go there. If not, go to the other half.

Approach:

  1. Use a closed window low = 0, high = n − 1 and loop while low ≤ high.
  2. If nums[middle] == target, return middle.
  3. If nums[low] ≤ nums[middle], the left half is sorted. If the target lies in [nums[low], nums[middle]), go left; otherwise go right.
  4. Otherwise the right half is sorted. If the target lies in (nums[middle], nums[high]], go right; otherwise go left.
  5. If the window becomes empty, return -1.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        # Closed window [low, high]: both ends are still candidates.
        low = 0
        high = len(nums) - 1

        while low <= high:
            # Look at the middle element.
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            # Lucky case: the middle element IS the target.
            if nums[middle] == target:
                return middle

            if nums[low] <= nums[middle]:
                # The LEFT half nums[low..middle] is sorted (no drop inside it).
                # In a sorted piece we can check "is target inside?" with its ends.
                if nums[low] <= target and target < nums[middle]:
                    # Target is inside the sorted left half: go left.
                    high = middle - 1
                else:
                    # Target is not there, so it must be in the right half.
                    low = middle + 1
            else:
                # Otherwise the RIGHT half nums[middle..high] is sorted.
                if nums[middle] < target and target <= nums[high]:
                    # Target is inside the sorted right half: go right.
                    low = middle + 1
                else:
                    # Target is not there, so it must be in the left half.
                    high = middle - 1

        # The window became empty: the target is not in the array.
        return -1
function search(nums: number[], target: number): number {
    // Closed window [low, high]: both ends are still candidates.
    let low = 0;
    let high = nums.length - 1;

    while (low <= high) {
        // Look at the middle element.
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        // Lucky case: the middle element IS the target.
        if (nums[middle] === target) {
            return middle;
        }

        if (nums[low] <= nums[middle]) {
            // The LEFT half nums[low..middle] is sorted (no drop inside it).
            // In a sorted piece we can check "is target inside?" with its ends.
            if (nums[low] <= target && target < nums[middle]) {
                // Target is inside the sorted left half: go left.
                high = middle - 1;
            } else {
                // Target is not there, so it must be in the right half.
                low = middle + 1;
            }
        } else {
            // Otherwise the RIGHT half nums[middle..high] is sorted.
            if (nums[middle] < target && target <= nums[high]) {
                // Target is inside the sorted right half: go right.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // Target is not there, so it must be in the left half.
                high = middle - 1;
            }
        }
    }

    // The window became empty: the target is not in the array.
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        // Closed window [low, high]: both ends are still candidates.
        int low = 0;
        int high = nums.length - 1;

        while (low <= high) {
            // Look at the middle element.
            int middle = (low + high) / 2;

            // Lucky case: the middle element IS the target.
            if (nums[middle] == target) {
                return middle;
            }

            if (nums[low] <= nums[middle]) {
                // The LEFT half nums[low..middle] is sorted (no drop inside it).
                // In a sorted piece we can check "is target inside?" with its ends.
                if (nums[low] <= target && target < nums[middle]) {
                    // Target is inside the sorted left half: go left.
                    high = middle - 1;
                } else {
                    // Target is not there, so it must be in the right half.
                    low = middle + 1;
                }
            } else {
                // Otherwise the RIGHT half nums[middle..high] is sorted.
                if (nums[middle] < target && target <= nums[high]) {
                    // Target is inside the sorted right half: go right.
                    low = middle + 1;
                } else {
                    // Target is not there, so it must be in the left half.
                    high = middle - 1;
                }
            }
        }

        // The window became empty: the target is not in the array.
        return -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. low = 0, high = len(nums) - 1: a closed window, both ends are still possible answers. The loop runs while the window is not empty (low <= high).
  2. Compute middle. If it holds the target, return it straight away.
  3. if nums[low] <= nums[middle]: the left part has no drop in it, so it is sorted. Its smallest value is nums[low] and its biggest is nums[middle]. If the target is between them, it can only be on the left (high = middle - 1); otherwise it can only be on the right (low = middle + 1).
  4. else: the drop is in the left part, so the right part middle..high is sorted. If the target is between nums[middle] (exclusive) and nums[high], go right (low = middle + 1); otherwise go left (high = middle - 1).
  5. If the loop ends without finding the target, return -1.

24651left [4..5] = 0..10 in [0, 1): high = 4
34440-nums[4] == 0: return 4

Edge cases to test:

  • No rotation at all.
  • Two elements, e.g. [3, 1].
  • The target is the first or last element, or is missing.

Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 34. Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Apple Array

Problem: In a sorted array (with duplicates), return [first, last] index of target, or [-1, -1]. Must be O(log n).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 8
Output: [3,4]
Example 2
Input: nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 6
Output: [-1,-1]

Constraints: 0 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · -10⁹ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · nums is a non-decreasing array. · -10⁹ ≤ target ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

Run binary search twice: once for the first position, once for the last.

Hint 2

"First index with nums[i] ≥ target" and "first index with nums[i] > target" give both ends.

From brute force to the pattern: Finding the target and then walking left and right is O(n) when the target repeats many times. Two lower-bound searches find both ends in O(log n).

Spot it: "first and last position" in a sorted array: two boundary searches.

Key insight: The first position is lower_bound(target), the first index with value ≥ target. The last position is one before lower_bound(target + 1). Same template, called twice.

Approach:

  1. Write first_index_at_least(goal): the first index with nums[i] ≥ goal (half-open template).
  2. first = first_index_at_least(target). If it's out of range or nums[first] != target, return [-1, -1].
  3. last = first_index_at_least(target + 1) − 1, the last index whose value is < target + 1.
  4. Return [first, last].
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def searchRange(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
        # Helper: the first index whose value is >= goal (the lower bound).
        def first_index_at_least(goal):
            low = 0
            high = len(nums)
            while low < high:
                middle = (low + high) // 2
                if nums[middle] < goal:
                    # Too small: the answer is to the right of middle.
                    low = middle + 1
                else:
                    # Big enough: middle might be the answer, keep it.
                    high = middle
            return low

        # Step 1: where does target start?
        first = first_index_at_least(target)

        # If that index is past the end, or holds a different number,
        # the target does not appear at all.
        if first == len(nums):
            return [-1, -1]
        if nums[first] != target:
            return [-1, -1]

        # Step 2: the first index holding something >= target + 1 is just
        # after the last copy of target, so step back by one.
        last = first_index_at_least(target + 1) - 1
        return [first, last]
function searchRange(nums: number[], target: number): number[] {
    // Helper: the first index whose value is >= goal (the lower bound).
    function firstIndexAtLeast(goal: number): number {
        let low = 0;
        let high = nums.length;
        while (low < high) {
            const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);
            if (nums[middle] < goal) {
                // Too small: the answer is to the right of middle.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // Big enough: middle might be the answer, keep it.
                high = middle;
            }
        }
        return low;
    }

    // Step 1: where does target start?
    const first = firstIndexAtLeast(target);

    // If that index is past the end, or holds a different number,
    // the target does not appear at all.
    if (first === nums.length) {
        return [-1, -1];
    }
    if (nums[first] !== target) {
        return [-1, -1];
    }

    // Step 2: the first index holding something >= target + 1 is just
    // after the last copy of target, so step back by one.
    const last = firstIndexAtLeast(target + 1) - 1;
    return [first, last];
}
class Solution {
    public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
        // Step 1: where does target start?
        int first = firstIndexAtLeast(nums, target);

        // If that index is past the end, or holds a different number,
        // the target does not appear at all.
        if (first == nums.length) {
            return new int[] {-1, -1};
        }
        if (nums[first] != target) {
            return new int[] {-1, -1};
        }

        // Step 2: the first index holding something >= target + 1 is just
        // after the last copy of target, so step back by one.
        int last = firstIndexAtLeast(nums, (long) target + 1) - 1;
        return new int[] {first, last};
    }

    // Helper: the first index whose value is >= goal (the lower bound).
    private int firstIndexAtLeast(int[] nums, long goal) {
        int low = 0;
        int high = nums.length;
        while (low < high) {
            int middle = (low + high) / 2;
            if (nums[middle] < goal) {
                // Too small: the answer is to the right of middle.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // Big enough: middle might be the answer, keep it.
                high = middle;
            }
        }
        return low;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. first_index_at_least(goal) is the lower-bound template from section 5: a half-open window [low, high) that keeps middle when nums[middle] >= goal and skips past it otherwise. It returns the first index whose value is at least goal (or len(nums) if none).
  2. first = first_index_at_least(target): if target is in the list, this is its first copy.
  3. Two safety checks: if first is len(nums) (everything was smaller) or nums[first] is some bigger number, the target is missing, so return [-1, -1].
  4. Because the numbers are whole numbers, "the first value ≥ target + 1" is the first value bigger than target. One step before it is the last copy of target: last = first_index_at_least(target + 1) - 1.
  5. Return both positions.

Dry run on the example nums = [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10], target = 8 (two calls to the helper):

goallowhighmiddlenums[middle]decision
806388 >= 8: high = 3
803177 < 8: low = 2
823277 < 8: low = 3 → returns 3, so first = 3
906388 < 9: low = 4
94651010 >= 9: high = 5
945488 < 9: low = 5 → returns 5, so last = 5 - 1 = 4

nums[3] == 8, so the checks pass and the answer is [3, 4].

Edge cases to test:

  • Target missing → [-1, -1].
  • An empty array.
  • Every element equals the target.

Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 153. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array Google Meta Amazon Array

Problem: Return the minimum of a rotated sorted array of distinct numbers in O(log n).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [3,4,5,1,2]
Output: 1
Explanation: The original array was [1,2,3,4,5] rotated 3 times.
Example 2
Input: nums = [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]
Output: 0
Explanation: The original array was [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] and it was rotated 4 times.

Constraints: n == nums.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 5000 · -5000 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 5000 · All the integers of nums are unique. · nums is sorted and rotated between 1 and n times.

Hint 1

Compare nums[mid] with nums[right]. What does that tell you about where the drop is?

Hint 2

If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.

From brute force to the pattern: min(nums) is O(n). The rotation point (the minimum) splits the array into two sorted runs, and comparing with the right end tells you which run mid is in: O(log n).

Spot it: The minimum is the "rotation point". Compared with the last element, the array looks like bigger, bigger, …, smaller, smaller: a yes/no boundary.

Key insight: If nums[mid] > nums[hi], mid is in the left (rotated-up) part and the minimum is strictly to its right. Otherwise mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or to its left. Compare with hi, not lo: comparing with lo fails on arrays that aren't rotated at all.

Approach:

  1. Window low = 0, high = n − 1, loop while low < high.
  2. If nums[middle] > nums[high], the drop (the minimum) is strictly to the right: low = middle + 1.
  3. Otherwise middle..high is sorted, so the minimum is at middle or to its left: high = middle.
  4. When low == high, return nums[low].
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        low = 0
        high = len(nums) - 1

        # Stop when one candidate is left (low == high).
        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            if nums[middle] > nums[high]:
                # middle is bigger than the right end, so the "drop" (the
                # minimum) is somewhere strictly to the right of middle.
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                # nums[middle..high] is sorted, so the minimum is middle
                # itself or something to its left.
                high = middle

        # Only one candidate is left: that is the minimum.
        return nums[low]
function findMin(nums: number[]): number {
    let low = 0;
    let high = nums.length - 1;

    // Stop when one candidate is left (low == high).
    while (low < high) {
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        if (nums[middle] > nums[high]) {
            // middle is bigger than the right end, so the "drop" (the
            // minimum) is somewhere strictly to the right of middle.
            low = middle + 1;
        } else {
            // nums[middle..high] is sorted, so the minimum is middle
            // itself or something to its left.
            high = middle;
        }
    }

    // Only one candidate is left: that is the minimum.
    return nums[low];
}
class Solution {
    public int findMin(int[] nums) {
        int low = 0;
        int high = nums.length - 1;

        // Stop when one candidate is left (low == high).
        while (low < high) {
            int middle = (low + high) / 2;

            if (nums[middle] > nums[high]) {
                // middle is bigger than the right end, so the "drop" (the
                // minimum) is somewhere strictly to the right of middle.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // nums[middle..high] is sorted, so the minimum is middle
                // itself or something to its left.
                high = middle;
            }
        }

        // Only one candidate is left: that is the minimum.
        return nums[low];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. low = 0, high = len(nums) - 1: the minimum could be anywhere.
  2. The loop runs while more than one candidate is left.
  3. If nums[middle] > nums[high], the numbers go down somewhere between middle and high (in a sorted stretch the left end is never bigger than the right end). That drop is where the minimum sits, so it is strictly right of middle: low = middle + 1.
  4. Otherwise nums[middle] <= nums[high], so middle..high is sorted and its smallest number is nums[middle]. The minimum is middle or somewhere to its left: high = middle.
  5. When one candidate is left, return its value.

343121 <= 2: high = 3

Now low == high == 3, so the answer is nums[3] = 1.

Edge cases to test:

  • No rotation → the first element.
  • A single element.
  • Two elements in either order.

Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 875. Koko Eating Bananas Google Meta Nvidia Amazon Microsoft Netflix Array

Problem: Koko eats at speed k bananas per hour, finishing at most one pile per hour (a pile of p takes ceil(p / k) hours). Find the minimum k that lets her finish all piles within h hours.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: piles = [3,6,7,11], h = 8
Output: 4
Example 2
Input: piles = [30,11,23,4,20], h = 5
Output: 30

Constraints: 1 ≤ piles.length ≤ 10⁴ · piles.length ≤ h ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ piles[i] ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

If Koko can finish at speed k, she can also finish at any faster speed. That's a monotonic yes/no condition.

Hint 2

Binary-search the smallest speed in 1..max(piles) for which the hours Σ ceil(pile / k) are ≤ h.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every speed from 1 upward is O(max(piles) · n). "Can finish at speed k?" flips from no to yes exactly once, so binary search over speeds needs only O(n log(max pile)).

Spot it: "minimum speed such that…". If speed k works, every faster speed works too. That's monotonic, so binary search on the answer over [1, max(piles)]. (See the second visualization above.)

Key insight: ok(k) = total hours at speed k ≤ h. Each check costs O(n), and we need only log(max pile) checks.

Approach:

  1. Search space: speeds [1, max(piles)]. The top speed always works.
  2. hours_needed(speed) = Σ ceil(pile / speed), computed with integers as (pile + speed − 1) // speed.
  3. If hours_needed(middle) ≤ h, middle is fast enough and the answer is ≤ middle: high = middle. Otherwise low = middle + 1.
  4. Return low, the slowest speed that still finishes on time.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles: List[int], h: int) -> int:
        # Helper: how many hours does Koko need at this speed?
        def hours_needed(speed):
            total_hours = 0
            for pile in piles:
                # ceil(pile / speed) using only integers:
                # (pile + speed - 1) // speed rounds the division UP.
                hours_for_pile = (pile + speed - 1) // speed
                total_hours = total_hours + hours_for_pile
            return total_hours

        # The slowest useful speed is 1. The fastest we ever need is the
        # biggest pile (then every pile takes exactly 1 hour).
        low = 1
        high = max(piles)

        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            if hours_needed(middle) <= h:
                # Fast enough. Maybe a slower speed works too: keep middle.
                high = middle
            else:
                # Too slow, so every slower speed is too slow as well.
                low = middle + 1

        # low is the slowest speed that still finishes within h hours.
        return low
function minEatingSpeed(piles: number[], h: number): number {
    // Helper: how many hours does Koko need at this speed?
    function hoursNeeded(speed: number): number {
        let totalHours = 0;
        for (const pile of piles) {
            // ceil(pile / speed): Math.ceil rounds the division UP.
            const hoursForPile = Math.ceil(pile / speed);
            totalHours = totalHours + hoursForPile;
        }
        return totalHours;
    }

    // The slowest useful speed is 1. The fastest we ever need is the
    // biggest pile (then every pile takes exactly 1 hour).
    let low = 1;
    let high = Math.max(...piles);

    while (low < high) {
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        if (hoursNeeded(middle) <= h) {
            // Fast enough. Maybe a slower speed works too: keep middle.
            high = middle;
        } else {
            // Too slow, so every slower speed is too slow as well.
            low = middle + 1;
        }
    }

    // low is the slowest speed that still finishes within h hours.
    return low;
}
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        // The slowest useful speed is 1. The fastest we ever need is the
        // biggest pile (then every pile takes exactly 1 hour).
        int low = 1;
        int high = 0;
        for (int pile : piles) {
            high = Math.max(high, pile);
        }

        while (low < high) {
            int middle = low + (high - low) / 2;

            if (hoursNeeded(piles, middle) <= h) {
                // Fast enough. Maybe a slower speed works too: keep middle.
                high = middle;
            } else {
                // Too slow, so every slower speed is too slow as well.
                low = middle + 1;
            }
        }

        // low is the slowest speed that still finishes within h hours.
        return low;
    }

    // Helper: how many hours does Koko need at this speed?
    // (long: the total can pass the int range)
    private long hoursNeeded(int[] piles, int speed) {
        long totalHours = 0;
        for (int pile : piles) {
            // ceil(pile / speed) using only integers:
            // (pile + speed - 1) / speed rounds the division UP.
            long hoursForPile = ((long) pile + speed - 1) / speed;
            totalHours = totalHours + hoursForPile;
        }
        return totalHours;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. hours_needed(speed) adds up, pile by pile, how many hours each pile takes. A pile of 7 at speed 3 takes 3 hours (3 + 3 + 1), which is 7 ÷ 3 rounded up. (pile + speed - 1) // speed does that rounding up with whole numbers only.
  2. low = 1 is the slowest possible speed. high = max(piles) always works: every pile then takes exactly 1 hour, and h is at least the number of piles.
  3. In the loop, try speed middle. If it finishes within h hours, it works, and maybe a slower speed works too: high = middle.
  4. If it needs more than h hours, it is too slow, and so is every slower speed: low = middle + 1.
  5. When low == high, that is the slowest speed that still finishes on time.

Dry run on the example piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8 (start: low = 1, high = 11):

lowhighmiddlehours_needed(middle)decision
111666 <= 8: high = 6
1631010 > 8: low = 4
46588 <= 8: high = 5
45488 <= 8: high = 4

Now low == high == 4, so the answer is 4.

Edge cases to test:

  • h equals the number of piles → the answer is max(piles).
  • A single pile.
  • Huge piles (use integer ceiling division: (p + k − 1) // k).

Complexity: O(n log M) time where M = max(piles), O(1) space.

Hard 410. Split Array Largest Sum Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Split nums (non-negative) into k non-empty contiguous pieces so that the largest piece-sum is as small as possible. Return that value.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [7,2,5,10,8], k = 2
Output: 18
Explanation: There are four ways to split nums into two subarrays. The best way is to split it into [7,2,5] and [10,8], where the largest sum among the two subarrays is only 18.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 2
Output: 9
Explanation: There are four ways to split nums into two subarrays. The best way is to split it into [1,2,3] and [4,5], where the largest sum among the two subarrays is only 9.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁶ · 1 ≤ k ≤ min(50, nums.length)

Hint 1

Guess a maximum allowed subarray sum. Can you check quickly whether k pieces are enough?

Hint 2

Greedy check: cut whenever adding the next number would exceed the cap. Binary-search the smallest cap that works.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every way to cut into k pieces is exponential; DP is O(k · n²). The answer lies in [max(nums), sum(nums)], and feasibility is monotonic in the cap, so binary search with a greedy check is O(n log(sum)).

Spot it: "minimize the largest sum" means "minimize the maximum", the classic binary-search-on-the-answer phrase. If a cap of X per piece is achievable with ≤ k pieces, any bigger cap is too.

Key insight: The answer lies between max(nums) (no piece can be smaller than the biggest element) and sum(nums) (one piece). For a guess cap, greedily pack elements left to right and start a new piece only when the next element would overflow. If that uses ≤ k pieces, cap is feasible.

Approach:

  1. Search space for the answer: [max(nums), sum(nums)].
  2. pieces_needed(cap): walk left to right and start a new piece whenever adding the next number would exceed cap.
  3. If pieces_needed(middle) ≤ k, the cap is feasible (you can always split further to use exactly k pieces): high = middle. Otherwise low = middle + 1.
  4. Return low, the smallest feasible cap.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def splitArray(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        # Helper: if no piece may sum to more than cap, how many pieces do we
        # need? Fill each piece greedily from left to right.
        def pieces_needed(cap):
            pieces = 1
            current_sum = 0
            for number in nums:
                if current_sum + number > cap:
                    # This number does not fit: close the piece, start a new one.
                    pieces = pieces + 1
                    current_sum = 0
                current_sum = current_sum + number
            return pieces

        # The answer is at least the biggest single number (it has to go in
        # some piece) and at most the total (everything in one piece).
        low = max(nums)
        high = sum(nums)

        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            if pieces_needed(middle) <= k:
                # This cap is achievable with k or fewer pieces: try smaller.
                high = middle
            else:
                # Needs too many pieces: the cap must be bigger.
                low = middle + 1

        # low is the smallest cap that works.
        return low
function splitArray(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    // Helper: if no piece may sum to more than cap, how many pieces do we
    // need? Fill each piece greedily from left to right.
    function piecesNeeded(cap: number): number {
        let pieces = 1;
        let currentSum = 0;
        for (const number of nums) {
            if (currentSum + number > cap) {
                // This number does not fit: close the piece, start a new one.
                pieces = pieces + 1;
                currentSum = 0;
            }
            currentSum = currentSum + number;
        }
        return pieces;
    }

    // The answer is at least the biggest single number (it has to go in
    // some piece) and at most the total (everything in one piece).
    let low = Math.max(...nums);
    let high = nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);

    while (low < high) {
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        if (piecesNeeded(middle) <= k) {
            // This cap is achievable with k or fewer pieces: try smaller.
            high = middle;
        } else {
            // Needs too many pieces: the cap must be bigger.
            low = middle + 1;
        }
    }

    // low is the smallest cap that works.
    return low;
}
class Solution {
    public int splitArray(int[] nums, int k) {
        // The answer is at least the biggest single number (it has to go in
        // some piece) and at most the total (everything in one piece).
        long low = 0;
        long high = 0;
        for (int number : nums) {
            low = Math.max(low, number);
            high = high + number;
        }

        while (low < high) {
            long middle = (low + high) / 2;

            if (piecesNeeded(nums, middle) <= k) {
                // This cap is achievable with k or fewer pieces: try smaller.
                high = middle;
            } else {
                // Needs too many pieces: the cap must be bigger.
                low = middle + 1;
            }
        }

        // low is the smallest cap that works.
        return (int) low;
    }

    // Helper: if no piece may sum to more than cap, how many pieces do we
    // need? Fill each piece greedily from left to right.
    private int piecesNeeded(int[] nums, long cap) {
        int pieces = 1;
        long currentSum = 0;
        for (int number : nums) {
            if (currentSum + number > cap) {
                // This number does not fit: close the piece, start a new one.
                pieces = pieces + 1;
                currentSum = 0;
            }
            currentSum = currentSum + number;
        }
        return pieces;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. pieces_needed(cap) starts with one piece whose running total current_sum is 0. For each number: if adding it would go over cap, close this piece (count one more piece, reset the total to 0). Then add the number to the current piece. It returns how many pieces were used.
  2. low = max(nums) because some piece must contain the biggest number. high = sum(nums) because one piece holding everything always works.
  3. In the loop, try the cap middle. If it needs k or fewer pieces, it is achievable (you could split pieces further to reach exactly k), so try smaller: high = middle.
  4. If it needs more than k pieces, the cap is too small: low = middle + 1.
  5. When low == high, that is the smallest achievable "largest piece sum".

Dry run on the example nums = [7, 2, 5, 10, 8], k = 2 (start: low = 10, high = 32):

lowhighmiddlepieces_needed(middle)decision
10322122 <= 2: high = 21
10211533 > 2: low = 16
16211822 <= 2: high = 18
16181733 > 2: low = 18

Now low == high == 18: the best split is [7, 2, 5] | [10, 8] with sums 14 and 18.

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 1 → the total sum.
  • k = n → the largest element.
  • Zeros in the array.

Complexity: O(n log S) time where S = sum(nums), O(1) space. (A DP solution is O(k·n²).)

8. Common mistakes

Infinite loopsWith while lo < hi and hi = mid, you must use lo = mid + 1 (never lo = mid). Otherwise, when hi = lo + 1, mid == lo forever.
Mixing window stylesPick one and stay consistent. Half-open [lo, hi): hi = len(nums), while lo < hi, hi = mid. Closed [lo, hi]: hi = len(nums) − 1, while lo <= hi, hi = mid − 1.
Wrong search range on the answerThe range must surely contain the answer: Koko [1, max(piles)], Split Array [max(nums), sum(nums)]. Starting Split Array at 0 makes the greedy check meaningless.
A non-monotonic checkBinary search silently returns garbage if ok isn't F…F T…T. Convince yourself: "if x works, does every bigger x work?"
Float ceil and overflow habitsUse (p + k − 1) // k instead of math.ceil(p / k) to avoid float error. In Java/C++, write mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2. Python ints don't overflow, but interviewers like to see that you know.

9. Self-check quiz

"Ship all packages within D days. What's the minimum ship capacity?" (LeetCode 1011)

"Minimum capacity such that it's feasible", and a bigger capacity is always feasible too. Search capacities in [max(weights), sum(weights)] with a greedy day-count check.

lower_bound([1, 3, 3, 5, 8], 4) returns…

The first index whose value is ≥ 4 is index 3 (value 5). Lower bound never returns -1; when target is bigger than everything, it returns len(nums).

Why does binary search still work on a rotated sorted array?

Any cut of a rotated sorted array leaves at least one half in order. You can range-check the target against that half and discard one side.

Template: while lo < hi, and if ok(mid): hi = mid. What goes in the else branch?

mid failed, so it can't be the answer; skip it. lo = mid can loop forever.

Easy 35. Search Insert Position Start here Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Given a sorted array of distinct numbers, return the index of target, or the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,3,5,6], target = 5
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,3,5,6], target = 2
Output: 1

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁴ · -10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴ · nums contains distinct values sorted in ascending order. · -10⁴ ≤ target ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

If the target isn't present, where would it go?

Hint 2

Find the first index with nums[i] ≥ target (lower bound).

From brute force to the pattern: A linear scan for the first element ≥ target is O(n). Lower-bound binary search finds the same index in O(log n).

Spot it: "Where would it go" is the first index with nums[i] ≥ target. That's exactly lower bound.

Approach:

  1. Half-open window [0, n).
  2. If nums[middle] < target, set low = middle + 1; else high = middle.
  3. Return low.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def searchInsert(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        # Half-open window [low, high). high starts at len(nums) because
        # the answer can be "insert at the very end".
        low = 0
        high = len(nums)

        while low < high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            if nums[middle] < target:
                # Too small: target belongs to the right of middle.
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                # nums[middle] >= target: middle is a valid spot,
                # but an earlier spot might be valid too.
                high = middle

        # low is the first index whose value is >= target.
        return low
function searchInsert(nums: number[], target: number): number {
    // Half-open window [low, high). high starts at nums.length because
    // the answer can be "insert at the very end".
    let low = 0;
    let high = nums.length;

    while (low < high) {
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        if (nums[middle] < target) {
            // Too small: target belongs to the right of middle.
            low = middle + 1;
        } else {
            // nums[middle] >= target: middle is a valid spot,
            // but an earlier spot might be valid too.
            high = middle;
        }
    }

    // low is the first index whose value is >= target.
    return low;
}
class Solution {
    public int searchInsert(int[] nums, int target) {
        // Half-open window [low, high). high starts at nums.length because
        // the answer can be "insert at the very end".
        int low = 0;
        int high = nums.length;

        while (low < high) {
            int middle = (low + high) / 2;

            if (nums[middle] < target) {
                // Too small: target belongs to the right of middle.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // nums[middle] >= target: middle is a valid spot,
                // but an earlier spot might be valid too.
                high = middle;
            }
        }

        // low is the first index whose value is >= target.
        return low;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. low = 0, high = len(nums): the answer is somewhere from 0 to len(nums). len(nums) means "after the last element".
  2. Each loop looks at middle. If nums[middle] is smaller than the target, the target must go after it: low = middle + 1.
  3. If nums[middle] is at least the target, putting the target at middle keeps the list sorted, but maybe an earlier spot also works. Keep middle and drop the right side: high = middle.
  4. When low == high, that index is the first value ≥ target: the target's position if present, or where it would be inserted.

Dry run on the example nums = [1, 3, 5, 6], target = 5:

lowhighmiddlenums[middle]decision
04255 >= 5: high = 2
02133 < 5: low = 2

Now low == high == 2, so the answer is 2.

Edge cases to test:

  • The target is smaller than everything → 0.
  • The target is larger than everything → n.
  • The target is present.

Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 162. Find Peak Element Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Netflix Array

Problem: Return the index of any element strictly greater than its neighbors. Treat nums[−1] and nums[n] as −∞. Adjacent values are never equal. Required: O(log n).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,1]
Output: 2
Explanation: 3 is a peak element and your function should return the index number 2.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,1,3,5,6,4]
Output: 5
Explanation: Your function can return either index number 1 where the peak element is 2, or index number 5 where the peak element is 6.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 1000 · -2³¹ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 2³¹ - 1 · nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i.

Hint 1

If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], you're on an uphill slope. Is there definitely a peak to the right?

Hint 2

Move toward the higher neighbour; since the ends count as −∞, a peak always exists in that direction.

From brute force to the pattern: Scanning for any element bigger than both neighbours is O(n). Walking toward the higher neighbour always keeps a peak inside the window, so binary search finds one in O(log n).

Spot it: The array isn't sorted, but comparing nums[mid] with nums[mid + 1] tells you which way is "uphill". Walking uphill always reaches a peak, because the edge is −∞.

Approach:

  1. Window low = 0, high = n − 1, loop while low < high.
  2. If nums[middle] < nums[middle + 1], you're on an upward slope, so a peak exists to the right: low = middle + 1.
  3. Otherwise you're on a downward slope (or at a peak), so a peak exists at middle or to its left: high = middle.
  4. Return low.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def findPeakElement(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        low = 0
        high = len(nums) - 1

        while low < high:
            # Because middle < high, middle + 1 is always a valid index.
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            if nums[middle] < nums[middle + 1]:
                # Going uphill to the right: a peak must exist on the right.
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                # Going downhill: middle or something to its left is a peak.
                high = middle

        # One candidate left: it is a peak.
        return low
function findPeakElement(nums: number[]): number {
    let low = 0;
    let high = nums.length - 1;

    while (low < high) {
        // Because middle < high, middle + 1 is always a valid index.
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        if (nums[middle] < nums[middle + 1]) {
            // Going uphill to the right: a peak must exist on the right.
            low = middle + 1;
        } else {
            // Going downhill: middle or something to its left is a peak.
            high = middle;
        }
    }

    // One candidate left: it is a peak.
    return low;
}
class Solution {
    public int findPeakElement(int[] nums) {
        int low = 0;
        int high = nums.length - 1;

        while (low < high) {
            // Because middle < high, middle + 1 is always a valid index.
            int middle = (low + high) / 2;

            if (nums[middle] < nums[middle + 1]) {
                // Going uphill to the right: a peak must exist on the right.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // Going downhill: middle or something to its left is a peak.
                high = middle;
            }
        }

        // One candidate left: it is a peak.
        return low;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. low = 0, high = len(nums) - 1: every index might be a peak.
  2. The loop runs while more than one candidate remains (low < high). Since middle rounds down, it is always less than high, so nums[middle + 1] never goes off the end.
  3. If the next number is bigger, we are walking uphill. Keep walking right and we must reach a peak (at worst the last element, since past the end counts as −∞). So drop middle and everything left of it: low = middle + 1.
  4. Otherwise the next number is smaller, so we are going downhill. Either middle is a peak or there is one to its left: high = middle.
  5. When one index is left, it is a peak.

Dry run on the example nums = [1, 2, 1, 3, 5, 6, 4]:

lowhighmiddlenums[middle]nums[middle + 1]decision
06335uphill: low = 4
46564downhill: high = 5
45456uphill: low = 5

Now low == high == 5: nums[5] = 6 is a peak (index 1 would also be accepted).

Edge cases to test:

  • A single element → index 0.
  • Strictly increasing → the last index.
  • Several peaks: any one is accepted.

Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 74. Search a 2D Matrix Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Matrix

Problem: Each row is sorted, and each row's first value is bigger than the previous row's last value. Return whether target is in the matrix.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: matrix = [[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]], target = 3
Output: true
Example 2
Input: matrix = [[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]], target = 13
Output: false

Constraints: m == matrix.length · n == matrix[i].length · 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 100 · -10⁴ ≤ matrix[i][j], target ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

Read the matrix row by row and it's one long sorted list.

Hint 2

Binary-search indices 0..rows·cols − 1 and map index i to matrix[i // cols][i % cols].

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every cell is O(r · c); searching each row is O(r log c). Treating the matrix as one sorted array gives O(log(r · c)).

Spot it: Read row by row, the matrix is one long sorted array. Binary search over flat indices 0 … R·C − 1 and convert each one to (row, col).

Approach:

  1. Closed window over flat indices [0, R·C − 1].
  2. Convert middle to a cell: row = middle // column_count, column = middle % column_count.
  3. Compare with the target and halve the window, as in classic binary search.
  4. Return False if the window empties.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def searchMatrix(self, matrix: List[List[int]], target: int) -> bool:
        row_count = len(matrix)
        column_count = len(matrix[0])

        # Pretend the matrix is one long sorted list with
        # row_count * column_count cells, numbered 0, 1, 2, ...
        low = 0
        high = row_count * column_count - 1

        while low <= high:
            middle = (low + high) // 2

            # Turn the flat position back into (row, column).
            row = middle // column_count
            column = middle % column_count
            value = matrix[row][column]

            if value == target:
                return True
            if value < target:
                # Too small: look in the later cells.
                low = middle + 1
            else:
                # Too big: look in the earlier cells.
                high = middle - 1

        # Window empty: the target is not in the matrix.
        return False
function searchMatrix(matrix: number[][], target: number): boolean {
    const rowCount = matrix.length;
    const columnCount = matrix[0].length;

    // Pretend the matrix is one long sorted array with
    // rowCount * columnCount cells, numbered 0, 1, 2, ...
    let low = 0;
    let high = rowCount * columnCount - 1;

    while (low <= high) {
        const middle = Math.floor((low + high) / 2);

        // Turn the flat position back into (row, column).
        const row = Math.floor(middle / columnCount);
        const column = middle % columnCount;
        const value = matrix[row][column];

        if (value === target) {
            return true;
        }
        if (value < target) {
            // Too small: look in the later cells.
            low = middle + 1;
        } else {
            // Too big: look in the earlier cells.
            high = middle - 1;
        }
    }

    // Window empty: the target is not in the matrix.
    return false;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean searchMatrix(int[][] matrix, int target) {
        int rowCount = matrix.length;
        int columnCount = matrix[0].length;

        // Pretend the matrix is one long sorted array with
        // rowCount * columnCount cells, numbered 0, 1, 2, ...
        int low = 0;
        int high = rowCount * columnCount - 1;

        while (low <= high) {
            int middle = (low + high) / 2;

            // Turn the flat position back into (row, column).
            int row = middle / columnCount;
            int column = middle % columnCount;
            int value = matrix[row][column];

            if (value == target) {
                return true;
            }
            if (value < target) {
                // Too small: look in the later cells.
                low = middle + 1;
            } else {
                // Too big: look in the earlier cells.
                high = middle - 1;
            }
        }

        // Window empty: the target is not in the matrix.
        return false;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. row_count and column_count record the matrix size.
  2. Reading the rows one after another gives one long sorted list. Its positions are 0 to row_count * column_count - 1, so that is our closed window [low, high].
  3. For each middle position, middle // column_count says how many full rows come before it (the row), and middle % column_count is what is left over (the column). That is the cell we read.
  4. If the cell equals the target, we are done. If it is smaller, the target can only be in later positions (low = middle + 1); if bigger, only in earlier ones (high = middle - 1).
  5. If the window becomes empty, the target is not there: return False.
