  • Many stores.
  • One type.

Complexity: O(m log(max)) time, O(1) space.

Medium 2080. Range Frequency Queries Amazon Microsoft ArrayHash Map

Problem: Design query(left, right, value): how many times value occurs in arr[left..right].

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: ["RangeFreqQuery", "query", "query"] [[[12, 33, 4, 56, 22, 2, 34, 33, 22, 12, 34, 56]], [1, 2, 4], [0, 11, 33]]
Output: [null, 1, 2]
Explanation: RangeFreqQuery rangeFreqQuery = new RangeFreqQuery([12, 33, 4, 56, 22, 2, 34, 33, 22, 12, 34, 56]); rangeFreqQuery.query(1, 2, 4); // return 1. The value 4 occurs 1 time in the subarray [33, 4] rangeFreqQuery.query(0, 11, 33); // return 2. The value 33 occurs 2 times in the whole array.

Constraints: 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ arr[i], value ≤ 10⁴ · 0 ≤ left ≤ right < arr.length · At most 10⁵ calls will be made to query

Hint 1

For a given value, where does it occur?

Hint 2

Count occurrences in a range with binary search.

From brute force to the pattern: Scanning per query is O(n); index lists + bisect are O(log n).

Spot it: Group indices by value in a hash map (they're collected in sorted order); a range count is two binary searches.

Why not another pattern? Scanning the range per query is O(n) each; a prefix count per value is O(n · distinct) memory.

Approach:

  1. Constructor: where[v] = list of indices with value v.
  2. query: bisect_right(where[v], right) − bisect_left(where[v], left).
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict

class RangeFreqQuery:
    def __init__(self, arr: List[int]):
        self.where = defaultdict(list)  # value -> indices, ascending
        for i, v in enumerate(arr):
            self.where[v].append(i)

    def query(self, left: int, right: int, value: int) -> int:
        idx = self.where.get(value, [])
        return bisect_right(idx, right) - bisect_left(idx, left)  # indices inside [left, right]
class RangeFreqQuery {
    private where = new Map<number, number[]>();  // value -> indices, ascending

    constructor(arr: number[]) {
        for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
            if (!this.where.has(arr[i])) {
                this.where.set(arr[i], []);
            }
            this.where.get(arr[i])!.push(i);
        }
    }

    query(left: number, right: number, value: number): number {
        const idx = this.where.get(value) ?? [];
        // first index with idx[i] > bound (or >= bound when strict is false)
        const firstAfter = (bound: number, strict: boolean): number => {
            let lo = 0;
            let hi = idx.length;
            while (lo < hi) {
                const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
                if (strict ? idx[mid] <= bound : idx[mid] < bound) {
                    lo = mid + 1;
                } else {
                    hi = mid;
                }
            }
            return lo;
        };
        return firstAfter(right, true) - firstAfter(left, false);  // indices inside [left, right]
    }
}
class RangeFreqQuery {
    private Map<Integer, List<Integer>> where = new HashMap<>();  // value -> indices, ascending

    public RangeFreqQuery(int[] arr) {
        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
            where.computeIfAbsent(arr[i], key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(i);
        }
    }

    public int query(int left, int right, int value) {
        List<Integer> idx = where.getOrDefault(value, List.of());
        return firstAfter(idx, right, true) - firstAfter(idx, left, false);  // indices inside [left, right]
    }

    // first position with idx[position] > bound (strict) or >= bound
    private int firstAfter(List<Integer> idx, int bound, boolean strict) {
        int lo = 0;
        int hi = idx.size();
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (strict ? idx.get(mid) <= bound : idx.get(mid) < bound) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }
        }
        return lo;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Indices are appended in increasing order, so each list is sorted.
  2. The two binary searches bracket exactly the indices in the range.

  • Value not in the array → 0.
  • left == right.
  • Whole-array query.

Complexity: O(n) to build, O(log n) per query, O(n) space.

Hard 2448. Minimum Cost to Make Array Equal Amazon Cisco Array

Problem: Changing nums[i] by 1 costs cost[i]. Return the minimum total cost to make all elements equal.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,3,5,2], cost = [2,3,1,14]
Output: 8
Explanation: We can make all the elements equal to 2 in the following way: - Increase the 0th element one time. The cost is 2. - Decrease the 1st element one time. The cost is 3. - Decrease the 2nd element three times. The cost is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. The total cost is 2 + 3 + 3 = 8. It can be shown that we cannot make the array equal with a smaller cost.
Example 2
Input: nums = [2,2,2,2,2], cost = [4,2,8,1,3]
Output: 0
Explanation: All the elements are already equal, so no operations are needed.

Constraints: n == nums.length == cost.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i], cost[i] ≤ 10⁶ · Test cases are generated in a way that the output doesn't exceed 2⁵³-1

Hint 1

Plot the total cost as a function of the target value. What shape is it?

Hint 2

A convex function's minimum can be found with binary search on the slope.

From brute force to the pattern: Every target value: O(n · range); binary search on the slope: O(n log range); weighted median: O(n log n).

Spot it: f(x) = Σ cost[i] · |nums[i] − x| is a sum of V-shapes, so it's convex: it decreases, then increases. Binary search for the first x where f(x + 1) ≥ f(x). (The optimum is the weighted median.)

Why not another pattern? Evaluating every x up to 10⁶ is O(n · range).

Approach:

  1. lo = min(nums), hi = max(nums).
  2. If f(mid) ≤ f(mid + 1), the minimum is at or left of mid; else right.
  3. Return f(lo).
class Solution:
    def minCost(self, nums: List[int], cost: List[int]) -> int:
        def total(x):
            return sum(c * abs(v - x) for v, c in zip(nums, cost))

        lo, hi = min(nums), max(nums)
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if total(mid) <= total(mid + 1):
                hi = mid  # not decreasing any more: the minimum is at or before mid
            else:
                lo = mid + 1  # still going down
        return total(lo)
function minCost(nums: number[], cost: number[]): number {
    // The cost totals can pass 2^53, so they are added up as BigInts.
    function total(x: number): bigint {
        let sum = 0n;
        for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            sum += BigInt(cost[i]) * BigInt(Math.abs(nums[i] - x));
        }
        return sum;
    }

    let lo = Math.min(...nums);
    let hi = Math.max(...nums);
    while (lo < hi) {
        const mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2);
        if (total(mid) <= total(mid + 1)) {
            hi = mid;  // not decreasing any more: the minimum is at or before mid
        } else {
            lo = mid + 1;  // still going down
        }
    }
    return Number(total(lo));
}
class Solution {
    public long minCost(int[] nums, int[] cost) {
        int lo = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int hi = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        for (int v : nums) {
            lo = Math.min(lo, v);
            hi = Math.max(hi, v);
        }
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (total(nums, cost, mid) <= total(nums, cost, mid + 1)) {
                hi = mid;  // not decreasing any more: the minimum is at or before mid
            } else {
                lo = mid + 1;  // still going down
            }
        }
        return total(nums, cost, lo);
    }

    private long total(int[] nums, int[] cost, int x) {
        long sum = 0;  // long: the cost totals pass the int range
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            sum += (long) cost[i] * Math.abs(nums[i] - x);
        }
        return sum;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each term c · |v − x| is convex, and sums of convex functions are convex.
  2. Comparing neighbours tells which side of the minimum mid is on.
  3. The optimum always lies between the smallest and largest value.

  • Already equal → 0.
  • One heavy cost dominates.
  • Large values (64-bit cost).

Complexity: O(n log(range)) time, O(1) space.

Hard 3661. Maximum Walls Destroyed by Robots Amazon Array

Problem: Each robot fires once, left or right, up to its distance; bullets stop at other robots. Maximise the number of distinct walls destroyed.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: robots = [4], distance = [3], walls = [1,10]
Output: 1
Explanation: robots[0] = 4 fires left with distance[0] = 3, covering [1, 4] and destroys walls[0] = 1. Thus, the answer is 1.
Example 2
Input: robots = [10,2], distance = [5,1], walls = [5,2,7]
Output: 3
Explanation: robots[0] = 10 fires left with distance[0] = 5, covering [5, 10] and destroys walls[0] = 5 and walls[2] = 7. robots[1] = 2 fires left with distance[1] = 1, covering [1, 2] and destroys walls[1] = 2. Thus, the answer is 3.

Constraints: 1 ≤ robots.length == distance.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ walls.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ robots[i], walls[j] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ distance[i] ≤ 10⁵ · All values in robots are unique · All values in walls are unique

Hint 1

Sort the robots. Which robots' bullets can hit the same wall?

Hint 2

Only neighbours interact: use a DP with the direction of the previous robot as the state.

Hint 3

Count walls in a position range with binary search.

From brute force to the pattern: All 2ⁿ direction choices is exponential; the 2-state DP is O(n log w).

Spot it: Sorted by position, a robot's bullet stays between its neighbours, so only adjacent robots interact (robot i − 1 firing right and robot i firing left can hit the same walls). That's a DP over robots with 2 states, and wall counts in a range come from binary search on the sorted walls.

Why not another pattern? Trying all 2ⁿ direction choices is exponential.

Approach:

  1. Sort robots by position, walls ascending; walls_in(a, b) = count of walls in [a, b] via bisect.
  2. L_i = [max(p_i − d_i, p_{i−1} + 1), p_i], R_i = [p_i, min(p_i + d_i, p_{i+1} − 1)].
  3. dpR[i] = |R_i| + max(dpL[i−1], dpR[i−1]); dpL[i] = |L_i| + max(dpL[i−1], dpR[i−1] − |R_{i−1} ∩ L_i|).
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right

class Solution:
    def maxWalls(self, robots: List[int], distance: List[int], walls: List[int]) -> int:
        bots = sorted(zip(robots, distance))
        walls = sorted(walls)
        n = len(bots)

        def walls_in(a, b):  # walls with a <= position <= b
            return bisect_right(walls, b) - bisect_left(walls, a) if a <= b else 0

        left_range, right_range = [], []
        for i, (p, d) in enumerate(bots):
            lo = max(p - d, bots[i - 1][0] + 1 if i else p - d)  # stops before the previous robot
            hi = min(p + d, bots[i + 1][0] - 1 if i + 1 < n else p + d)  # and before the next one
            left_range.append((lo, p))
            right_range.append((p, hi))
        dp_l = walls_in(*left_range[0])  # best so far if robot i fires left
        dp_r = walls_in(*right_range[0])  # ... or right
        for i in range(1, n):
            (a1, b1), (a2, b2) = right_range[i - 1], left_range[i]
            shared = walls_in(max(a1, a2), min(b1, b2))  # walls both bullets would hit
            new_l = walls_in(*left_range[i]) + max(dp_l, dp_r - shared)
            new_r = walls_in(*right_range[i]) + max(dp_l, dp_r)
            dp_l, dp_r = new_l, new_r
        return max(dp_l, dp_r)
function maxWalls(robots: number[], distance: number[], walls: number[]): number {
    const bots = robots.map((p, i) => [p, distance[i]]).sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1]);
    walls = [...walls].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const n = bots.length;

    // first index with walls[index] > bound (strict) or >= bound
    function firstAfter(bound: number, strict: boolean): number {
        let lo = 0;
        let hi = walls.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
            if (strict ? walls[mid] <= bound : walls[mid] < bound) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }
        }
        return lo;
    }

    // walls with a <= position <= b
    const wallsIn = (a: number, b: number): number => (a <= b ? firstAfter(b, true) - firstAfter(a, false) : 0);

    const leftRange: [number, number][] = [];
    const rightRange: [number, number][] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        const [p, d] = bots[i];
        const lo = Math.max(p - d, i > 0 ? bots[i - 1][0] + 1 : p - d);  // stops before the previous robot
        const hi = Math.min(p + d, i + 1 < n ? bots[i + 1][0] - 1 : p + d);  // and before the next one
        leftRange.push([lo, p]);
        rightRange.push([p, hi]);
    }
    let dpL = wallsIn(...leftRange[0]);  // best so far if robot i fires left
    let dpR = wallsIn(...rightRange[0]);  // ... or right
    for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        const [a1, b1] = rightRange[i - 1];
        const [a2, b2] = leftRange[i];
        const shared = wallsIn(Math.max(a1, a2), Math.min(b1, b2));  // walls both bullets would hit
        const newL = wallsIn(...leftRange[i]) + Math.max(dpL, dpR - shared);
        const newR = wallsIn(...rightRange[i]) + Math.max(dpL, dpR);
        dpL = newL;
        dpR = newR;
    }
    return Math.max(dpL, dpR);
}
class Solution {
    private int[] walls;

    public int maxWalls(int[] robots, int[] distance, int[] walls) {
        int n = robots.length;
        int[][] bots = new int[n][];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            bots[i] = new int[] {robots[i], distance[i]};
        }
        Arrays.sort(bots, (a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]) : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        this.walls = walls.clone();
        Arrays.sort(this.walls);

        long[][] leftRange = new long[n][];
        long[][] rightRange = new long[n][];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            long p = bots[i][0], d = bots[i][1];
            long lo = Math.max(p - d, i > 0 ? bots[i - 1][0] + 1 : p - d);  // stops before the previous robot
            long hi = Math.min(p + d, i + 1 < n ? bots[i + 1][0] - 1 : p + d);  // and before the next one
            leftRange[i] = new long[] {lo, p};
            rightRange[i] = new long[] {p, hi};
        }
        int dpL = wallsIn(leftRange[0][0], leftRange[0][1]);  // best so far if robot i fires left
        int dpR = wallsIn(rightRange[0][0], rightRange[0][1]);  // ... or right
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            long a1 = rightRange[i - 1][0], b1 = rightRange[i - 1][1];
            long a2 = leftRange[i][0], b2 = leftRange[i][1];
            int shared = wallsIn(Math.max(a1, a2), Math.min(b1, b2));  // walls both bullets would hit
            int newL = wallsIn(a2, b2) + Math.max(dpL, dpR - shared);
            int newR = wallsIn(rightRange[i][0], rightRange[i][1]) + Math.max(dpL, dpR);
            dpL = newL;
            dpR = newR;
        }
        return Math.max(dpL, dpR);
    }

    // walls with a <= position <= b
    private int wallsIn(long a, long b) {
        return a <= b ? firstAfter(b, true) - firstAfter(a, false) : 0;
    }

    // first index with walls[index] > bound (strict) or >= bound
    private int firstAfter(long bound, boolean strict) {
        int lo = 0;
        int hi = walls.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (strict ? walls[mid] <= bound : walls[mid] < bound) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }
        }
        return lo;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A bullet can't pass a robot, so robot i only covers walls between its neighbours, including walls at its own position.
  2. Only robot i − 1 firing right and robot i firing left can overlap; the DP subtracts that overlap once.
  3. Each range count is two binary searches on the sorted walls.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Walls at robot positions.
  • A robot right next to another (range cut off).
  • No walls in range.

Complexity: O((n + w) log(n + w)) time, O(n) space.

Hard 3920. Maximize Fixed Points After Deletions Amazon Array

Problem: Delete any elements; positions shift left. Maximise the number of positions i with nums[i] == i afterwards.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [0,2,1]
Output: 2
Explanation: Delete nums[1] = 2. The array becomes [0, 1]. Now, nums[0] = 0 and nums[1] = 1, so both indices are fixed points. Thus, the answer is 2.
Example 2
Input: nums = [3,1,2]
Output: 2
Explanation: Do not delete any elements. The array remains [3, 1, 2]. Here, nums[1] = 1 and nums[2] = 2, so these indices are fixed points. Thus, the answer is 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵

Hint 1

For element i to become fixed at position nums[i], how many elements before it must be deleted?

Hint 2

Two kept elements must have increasing values and non-decreasing deletion counts.

Hint 3

Sort by one key and take a longest increasing subsequence on the other.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating deletions is exponential; the LIS view is O(n log n).

Spot it: Keeping nums[i] = v as a fixed point needs exactly i − v ≥ 0 deletions before it. Two kept points (i₁, v₁), (i₂, v₂) need v₁ < v₂ and i₁ − v₁ ≤ i₂ − v₂ (deletions only accumulate). Sort by d = i − v, then it's a strictly increasing LIS on v, solved with binary search.

Why not another pattern? Trying deletion sets is exponential; an O(n²) LIS is too slow for 10⁵.

Approach:

  1. Candidates (d, v) with d = i − nums[i] ≥ 0.
  2. Sort by (d, v).
  3. Patience-sorting LIS (strict) on v with bisect_left.
from bisect import bisect_left

class Solution:
    def maxFixedPoints(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        cands = sorted((i - v, v) for i, v in enumerate(nums) if v <= i)  # (deletions needed before it, value)
        tails = []  # tails[t]: smallest last value of a chain of length t + 1
        for _, v in cands:
            pos = bisect_left(tails, v)  # strictly increasing values
            if pos == len(tails):
                tails.append(v)
            else:
                tails[pos] = v
        return len(tails)
function maxFixedPoints(nums: number[]): number {
    // [deletions needed before it, value], for values that can become fixed points
    const cands: [number, number][] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] <= i) {
            cands.push([i - nums[i], nums[i]]);
        }
    }
    cands.sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1]);
    const tails: number[] = [];  // tails[t]: smallest last value of a chain of length t + 1
    for (const [, v] of cands) {
        // strictly increasing values: first tail >= v (binary search)
        let lo = 0;
        let hi = tails.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
            if (tails[mid] < v) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }
        }
        if (lo === tails.length) {
            tails.push(v);
        } else {
            tails[lo] = v;
        }
    }
    return tails.length;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxFixedPoints(int[] nums) {
        // (deletions needed before it, value), for values that can become fixed points
        List<int[]> cands = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (nums[i] <= i) {
                cands.add(new int[] {i - nums[i], nums[i]});
            }
        }
        cands.sort((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]) : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        int[] tails = new int[cands.size()];  // tails[t]: smallest last value of a chain of length t + 1
        int size = 0;
        for (int[] c : cands) {
            int v = c[1];
            // strictly increasing values: first tail >= v (binary search)
            int lo = 0;
            int hi = size;
            while (lo < hi) {
                int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
                if (tails[mid] < v) {
                    lo = mid + 1;
                } else {
                    hi = mid;
                }
            }
            tails[lo] = v;
            if (lo == size) {
                size++;
            }
        }
        return size;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If v₁ < v₂ and d₁ ≤ d₂, then i₁ = v₁ + d₁ < i₂, so the order in the array is right too.
  2. Sorting by d (ties by v) makes any increasing subsequence of v a valid set of fixed points.
  3. The tails array gives the LIS length in O(n log n).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already fixed points (d = 0).
  • Values larger than their index (never usable).
  • Equal values (only one can be kept).

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 475. Heaters Microsoft Array

Problem: Return the minimum radius so that every house is within that distance of some heater.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: houses = [1,2,3], heaters = [2]
Output: 1
Explanation: The only heater was placed in the position 2, and if we use the radius 1 standard, then all the houses can be warmed.
Example 2
Input: houses = [1,2,3,4], heaters = [1,4]
Output: 1
Explanation: The two heaters were placed at positions 1 and 4. We need to use a radius 1 standard, then all the houses can be warmed.

Constraints: 1 ≤ houses.length, heaters.length ≤ 3 * 10⁴ · 1 ≤ houses[i], heaters[i] ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

What does each house need?

Hint 2

Find each house's nearest heater with binary search.

From brute force to the pattern: All pairs: O(nm); binary search: O(n log m).

Spot it: Each house needs its nearest heater: sort heaters and binary search each house's position; the radius is the worst nearest distance.

Why not another pattern? Checking every house against every heater is O(n · m).

Approach:

  1. Sort heaters.
  2. For each house: i = bisect_left(heaters, h); nearest = min distance to heaters[i − 1] and heaters[i].
  3. Answer = max over houses.
from bisect import bisect_left

class Solution:
    def findRadius(self, houses: List[int], heaters: List[int]) -> int:
        heaters = sorted(heaters)
        radius = 0
        for h in houses:
            i = bisect_left(heaters, h)  # first heater at or right of the house
            right = heaters[i] - h if i < len(heaters) else float("inf")
            left = h - heaters[i - 1] if i > 0 else float("inf")
            radius = max(radius, min(left, right))  # this house's nearest heater
        return radius
function findRadius(houses: number[], heaters: number[]): number {
    heaters = [...heaters].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    let radius = 0;
    for (const h of houses) {
        // first heater at or right of the house (binary search)
        let lo = 0;
        let hi = heaters.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
            if (heaters[mid] < h) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }
        }
        const i = lo;
        const right = i < heaters.length ? heaters[i] - h : Infinity;
        const left = i > 0 ? h - heaters[i - 1] : Infinity;
        radius = Math.max(radius, Math.min(left, right));  // this house's nearest heater
    }
    return radius;
}
class Solution {
    public int findRadius(int[] houses, int[] heaters) {
        heaters = heaters.clone();
        Arrays.sort(heaters);
        int radius = 0;
        for (int h : houses) {
            // first heater at or right of the house (binary search)
            int lo = 0;
            int hi = heaters.length;
            while (lo < hi) {
                int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
                if (heaters[mid] < h) {
                    lo = mid + 1;
                } else {
                    hi = mid;
                }
            }
            int i = lo;
            int right = i < heaters.length ? heaters[i] - h : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
            int left = i > 0 ? h - heaters[i - 1] : Integer.MAX_VALUE;
            radius = Math.max(radius, Math.min(left, right));  // this house's nearest heater
        }
        return radius;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The nearest heater is one of the two neighbours in sorted order.
  2. The radius must cover the house whose nearest heater is farthest.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Houses outside all heaters.
  • A heater on a house.
  • One heater.

Complexity: O((n + m) log m) time, O(1) extra space.
